text:
Because it was always a stunt. The EV1 was intended to fail - it was a public display for the California state government by which GM could prove they were committed to zero-emission vehicles. A display with GM deliberately sabotaged, as their management knew that such a vehicle couldn't be justified commercially - they made a bare minimum of them to meet state requirements, and never sold any - only leased them under a temporary pilot program, for as long as it took for an association of car manufacturers to sue California and get a court to rule that California's emissions regulation laws were an unconstitional violation of the commerce clause. Then GM promptly cancelled the leases, destroyed most of the cars, and destroyed the internal components of the rest before donating the empty shells to museums as monuments to GM's green credentials.

The EV1 is an important momen in history - but not in the history of electric vehicles. It's important in the history of how influential corporations used PR campaigns, aggressive legal action and political pressure to fight against conservation measures that threatened their profits.
